key_terms.meaning: Element with v = iR; it converts electrical energy to heat and stores nothing. Unit: ohm (Ω).
Element with v = L di/dt; it stores energy in a magnetic field as ½Li². Unit: henry (H).
Element with i = C dv/dt; it stores energy in an electric field as ½Cv². Unit: farad (F).
Terminal voltage stays fixed at V whatever current the load draws; its v-i line is horizontal.
Source whose value is a fixed constant times another voltage or current in the circuit, written kV_x or kI_x (k has no unit).
At any node, Σ currents in = Σ currents out; algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero.
Round any closed loop, the algebraic sum of voltages is zero: Σ v = 0.
For resistors in series, v_k = V × R_k / R_total, where R_total is the sum of all series resistances.
For two resistors in parallel, I₁ = I × R₂/(R₁ + R₂), with I the total current entering the pair.
A voltage source V in series with R equals a current source I = V/R in parallel with the same R, as seen at the terminals.
Any three-terminal star of resistors can be replaced by an equivalent delta, and the reverse, using R_A = (R₁R₂ + R₂R₃ + R₃R₁)/R₁ and similar forms.
A fictitious current assumed to circulate round one window of a planar network; the branch current is the mesh current or the difference of two.
Voltage of a node measured with respect to one chosen reference node whose voltage is set to 0 V.
A loop formed by joining two meshes that share a current source, used when the source has an unknown voltage across it.
A closed surface enclosing two nodes joined by a voltage source, used in node analysis when the source has an unknown current through it.
Circuit of R, L, C and independent or dependent sources only, where doubling every source doubles every response and superposition holds.
In a linear circuit, the response to several independent sources is the sum of the responses to each source acting alone, the others set to zero.
Any linear two-terminal network reduces to a voltage source V_th in series with a resistance R_th, where V_th is the open-circuit voltage and R_th the resistance seen looking back.
The same network reduces to a current source I_N in parallel with R_th, where I_N is the short-circuit current and I_N = V_th/R_th.
Load receives maximum power when R_L = R_th, and that maximum is P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).

takeaways: Every lumped element is one fixed relation between its own voltage and current; R, L and C differ only in which of the two is differentiated.
An ideal source fixes one quantity and lets the other be whatever the load demands, which is why shorting an ideal voltage source or opening an ideal current source is harmless.
KCL is charge conservation at a node and KVL is energy conservation round a loop; together with Ohm's law they solve any DC network.
Series-parallel reduction, dividers, source transformation and star-delta are all bookkeeping tricks that replace a network by a simpler one with identical terminal behaviour.
Mesh analysis writes KVL, node analysis writes KCL; choose mesh when the circuit has many current sources or few windows, node when it has many voltage sources or few nodes.
Superposition, Thevenin, Norton and maximum power transfer all depend on linearity, and all fail once a diode, a saturated amplifier or a nonlinear load enters.
A dependent source does not break Thevenin's theorem, but it can make R_th negative, so the maximum power transfer condition needs a physical check.
Two solutions by different methods must agree; the examiner reads that agreement as proof of correctness, not as extra work.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are mostly solve-the-network questions, so full marks come from a labelled circuit diagram, stated method, visible equations and a boxed answer with units, plus one line of comment when the question says discuss or compare.

bank.q: Define an ideal voltage source and an ideal current source, draw their v-i characteristics, and explain why a real source such as a battery or a laboratory supply is represented by a practical source with an internal resistance.
outline: Ideal voltage source: voltage fixed at V, current set entirely by the load, v-i line horizontal.
Ideal current source: current fixed at I, voltage set by the load, v-i line vertical.
Real source: internal resistance in series (voltage source) or in parallel (current source) explains the drop of terminal voltage with load.
Practically, ideal sources cannot exist because any real device has finite internal impedance and finite power rating.
Practical voltage source must not be shorted and a practical current source must not be opened.

bank.q: Write the voltage-current relations for a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor, state the unit of each element, and explain which element stores energy and in what form. Give the stored-energy expressions.
outline: Resistor: v = iR, unit ohm, dissipates energy as heat, stores none.
Inductor: v = L di/dt, unit henry, stores ½Li² in a magnetic field, current cannot change instantly.
Capacitor: i = C dv/dt, unit farad, stores ½Cv² in an electric field, voltage cannot change instantly.
Each element is completely described by this one relation, which is what makes it a lumped element.
Sign conventions: passive sign convention, current enters the positive terminal of the voltage.

bank.q: State Kirchhoff's current law and Kirchhoff's voltage law. Explain the physical law behind each and show, with a simple two-loop circuit, how the two laws together give enough equations to find all currents.
outline: KCL: sum of currents entering a node equals sum leaving; algebraic sum at a node is zero.
KCL is conservation of charge at a point.
KVL: algebraic sum of voltages round a closed loop is zero.
KVL is conservation of energy: charge returning to its starting potential gains no net energy.
Count of independent equations: (n − 1) node equations and (b − n + 1) loop equations.
Worked two-loop example with the signs of the assumed current directions clearly marked.

bank.q: Derive the voltage divider rule for three resistors in series and the current divider rule for two resistors in parallel. State two practical uses of each rule.
outline: Series: same current through all; V_k = I R_k and I = V/R_total, giving V_k = V R_k/R_total.
Parallel: same voltage across all; I₁ = V/R₁ with V = I R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂), giving I₁ = I R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
Note that the current divider puts the other branch resistance in the numerator.
Uses: setting a bias voltage from a supply, measuring a high voltage with a series multiplier, splitting current between parallel branches, shunt ammeter.

bank.q: State the superposition theorem, Thevenin's theorem, Norton's theorem and the maximum power transfer theorem. For each, state the single condition on the circuit that must hold for it to apply.
outline: Superposition: response = sum of single-source responses, other independent sources set to zero (voltage source shorted, current source opened).
Thevenin: V_th = open-circuit voltage, R_th = resistance looking back with sources dead; series combination.
Norton: I_N = short-circuit current, R_th in parallel; I_N = V_th/R_th.
Maximum power transfer: R_L = R_th, P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).
Condition for all four: the circuit must be linear — no diodes, no saturated devices, no nonlinear loads.
Dependent sources must be kept alive when the independent sources are set to zero.

bank.q: A 24 V supply feeds 12 Ω in series with a parallel pair of 20 Ω and 30 Ω, and a 6 Ω resistor is connected across the 12 Ω resistor by a link of negligible resistance. Draw the circuit, reduce it step by step, and find the total current, the current in each 20 Ω and 30 Ω branch, and the power lost in the 12 Ω resistor.
outline: Correctly redraw the circuit, noting that the 6 Ω is in parallel with the 12 Ω.
Parallel pair 12 || 6 = 4 Ω.
Parallel pair 20 || 30 = 12 Ω.
Total resistance = 4 + 12 = 16 Ω; total current = 24/16 = 1.5 A.
Voltage across the 12 || 6 group = 1.5 × 4 = 6 V; current in 12 Ω = 0.5 A.
Current divider gives 20 Ω branch 0.9 A and 30 Ω branch 0.6 A.
Power in 12 Ω = 0.5² × 12 = 3 W, with units stated.

bank.q: A delta-connected set of resistors of 6 Ω, 12 Ω and 18 Ω is to be replaced by a star. Find the three star arms, then use the result to find the resistance between two corners of the original delta and check the answer against a direct calculation.
outline: Delta to star: R_A = R_AB R_CA/(R_AB + R_BC + R_CA) and the two cyclic forms.
Sum of delta resistors = 36 Ω; star arms = 2 Ω, 6 Ω and 3 Ω.
Resistance between the corners where 6 Ω and 12 Ω meet: 12 || (6 + 18) directly.
Via star: 2 + (6 || 3) must give the same number.
Both give the same value — this is the point of the test.
Comment that the star-delta swap does not change terminal behaviour, only the arithmetic.

bank.q: For a two-window planar network containing one voltage source in the outer branch and a current source shared by the two windows, write the mesh equations using a supermesh, and solve for both mesh currents.
outline: Draw and label the two mesh currents with assumed clockwise directions.
Constraint equation from the shared current source.
KVL round the supermesh, treating it as one loop.
KVL round the remaining ordinary mesh.
Solve the two simultaneous equations, showing the determinant or elimination steps.
Check by writing KCL at one node and confirming the same currents.

bank.q: For a network of four resistors and a 10 V source with a 5 V source connected directly between two non-reference nodes, use node voltage analysis with a supernode to find all node voltages and the current supplied by the 10 V source.
outline: Choose the reference node and label node voltages v₁, v₂, v₃.
Supernode enclosing the two nodes joined by the 5 V source.
Constraint equation v₂ − v₃ = 5.
KCL for the supernode as a whole, plus KCL at the remaining nodes.
Solve the equations and state all node voltages with units.
Current supplied = (10 − v₁)/series resistance, sign explained.

bank.q: A circuit contains a 12 V independent source, a 2 A independent source and a current-controlled voltage source 3I_x. Find the Thevenin equivalent across the terminals of a 4 Ω load, then find the load current.
outline: Compute V_th as the open-circuit voltage, keeping the dependent source in place.
Find I_x from the open-circuit condition, not from the loaded circuit.
Compute R_th by applying a test source of 1 V or 1 A at the terminals with independent sources dead and the dependent source alive.
R_th = V_test/I_test; state whether it is positive or negative and what a negative value would mean physically.
Reconnect the load: I_L = V_th/(R_th + 4).
Note that superposition can be used for V_th but never for R_th as a direct sum of resistances.

bank.q: A source of 20 V with an internal resistance of 5 Ω feeds a variable load. Find the load resistance for maximum power, the maximum power, the terminal voltage and the efficiency at that point.
outline: R_L = R_th = 5 Ω.
Total resistance 10 Ω, current 2 A.
P_max = I²R_L = 20 W, or V_th²/(4R_th) = 400/20 = 20 W, both agreeing.
Terminal voltage = 10 V, exactly half the source voltage.
Efficiency = 50 percent — the reason power systems are not designed at maximum power transfer.
Sketch of P_L against R_L showing the peak at R_L = R_th.

bank.q: A two-source resistive circuit is given. Solve it twice: once by superposition and once by Thevenin's theorem applied to the branch whose current is asked for. Compare the two answers, and say which method you would choose if the load resistance were to be varied over a range, with reasons.
outline: Superposition: kill each source in turn, compute the branch current, add with signs.
Thevenin: open-circuit voltage and R_th looking into the load terminals, then I = V_th/(R_th + R_L).
Both answers identical, which validates the work.
Superposition needs one full solution per source and gives one load condition only.
Thevenin gives one equivalent that answers every load value in one line, so it is preferred when the load varies.
Note that a nonlinear load would break both methods.

bank.q: Using mesh analysis, node analysis and superposition, find the same branch current in a three-mesh circuit of your choice, and compare the number of simultaneous equations each method needs. State a rule for choosing a method from the circuit topology alone.
outline: Count windows and nodes; the smaller count usually wins.
Mesh: b − n + 1 equations; node: n − 1 equations.
Superposition: one full solution per independent source, useful only for a few sources and a single wanted quantity.
All three results must agree; show at least one cross-check.
Current sources favour mesh with a supermesh; voltage sources favour node with a supernode.
Final recommendation with a reason, not a memorised sentence.

bank.q: A student claims that maximum power transfer always gives the most efficient operating point for a circuit. Examine the claim using a source of V_th and R_th feeding a load, derive P_L and the efficiency as functions of R_L, and state the practical design rule that follows.
outline: P_L = V_th²R_L/(R_th + R_L)²; differentiate and set to zero, giving R_L = R_th.
P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).
Efficiency = R_L/(R_th + R_L), which is 0.5 at maximum power and rises towards 1 as R_L grows.
So maximum power and maximum efficiency occur at different loads.
Communication and power systems choose R_L ≫ R_th for efficiency; electronic and signal circuits choose matching for power.
Conclusion: the claim is false as stated; the correct statement names the quantity being maximised.

glossary.def: A two-terminal device with a defined voltage-current relation, treated as a single lumped component.
An element whose physical size is small compared with the wavelength of the signals, so its behaviour can be described by one relation between terminal voltage and current.
Element in which v = iR, dissipating electrical energy as heat.
Element in which v = L di/dt, storing energy in a magnetic field.
Element in which i = C dv/dt, storing energy in an electric field.
Unit of resistance, equal to one volt per ampere.
Unit of inductance, equal to one volt-second per ampere.
Unit of capacitance, equal to one coulomb per volt.
A point in a circuit where two or more elements meet; all points joined by ideal wire form one node.
Any closed path through a circuit that returns to its starting node without repeating a branch.
A loop that contains no other loop inside it, i.e. one window of a planar circuit.
The node chosen as 0 V in node analysis, against which all other node voltages are measured.
A source whose voltage or current is fixed regardless of the load connected to it.
A source whose value is a fixed multiple of another voltage or current in the circuit.
A circuit made only of resistances, inductances, capacitances and independent or dependent sources, obeying superposition.
The voltage appearing across two terminals when nothing is connected between them; it equals V_th.
The current that flows through an ideal wire joining two terminals; it equals I_N.
The resistance seen looking into two terminals with all independent sources set to zero and dependent sources left in place.
Replacing a voltage source in series with a resistance by a current source in parallel with the same resistance, or the reverse.
Three elements joined at one common point, each free end forming a terminal of the three-terminal network.
Three elements joined end to end in a closed triangle, the three corners forming the terminals.
Rate of energy transfer, p = vi, measured in watts.
Ratio of power delivered to the load to total power supplied by the source, usually given as a percentage.
